Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Conveyancing fraud tends to take place at the end of a home sale. Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty Images Scam watch Property ‘Friday afternoon fraud’: warning for UK homebuyers on bank scams Victims have lost tens of thousands – and in one case £300,000 – due to fake emails from solicitor or estate agent Hilary Osborne Sun 23 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 02.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Y ou are poised to move house and are awaiting the solicitor’s instructions that things are ready to go and it is time to hand over your deposit. When the email arrives giving you their bank details, you set up the transfer and move the cash. And then the solicitor calls to ask where the money is. Conveyancing fraud involves criminals getting access to an email chain between homebuyers and their solicitors or estate agents and requesting payment to a bank account they control. Sometimes the solicitor has been hacked, but often the homebuyer has been the victim of a phishing exercise. The scam is sometimes known as “Friday afternoon fraud” as it tends to take place at the end of a sale, which is often timed before a weekend. The sums of money involved in a property sale mean the fraudster only have to land a few victims to make a lot of cash. Report Fraud (formerly known as Action Fraud) says there were 3,657 scams involving persuading people to pay into the wrong bank account in the 2025-26 financial year, and these cost victims a total of £101m. Conveyancing fraud is a subset of this. Between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025 Report Fraud recorded 140 property cases with an average loss of £78,393. In the worst case the Guardian has covered, a homebuyer transferred the entire £300,000 purchase price to the wrong account. City of London police has warned that this type of fraud isn’t limited to purchases – it’s also been reported by renters who have lost money they thought they’d paid to their letting agent, and in probate transactions. What it looks like The message looks just like an email from your solicitor or estate agent. It asks for you to make a payment you are expecting to make but may come earlier than you were expecting. It may say that the solicitors’ firm has new bank details and the payment needs to be made quickly. View image in fullscreen The fake email from the solicitor will say that the payment needs to be made quickly. Photograph: Tetra Images/Getty Images/Tetra images RF If your solicitor’s email has been hacked the message could come from its genuine address, but usually the fraudsters will be using a spoofed email address so if you look carefully you may spot something slightly different from the genuine company’s one. There may be a missing letter or extra punctuation mark, for example. What to do (and not do) Don’t post about your impending move on social media as fraudsters could spot this and realise that you are a good person to target. Make sure your side of the email chain is secure by setting a strong password for your account and using any extra protection that’s offered, such as two-factor authentication. Avoid logging into public wifi and using it to check your emails as this gives fraudsters a potential access point. If you are expecting to exchange on a property soon, make sure you have asked for the solicitor’s bank details either in person or over the phone in a call that you have made to it. Any message suggesting your solicitor has changed its bank details should be checked out – again ask them in person or by phone. Take heed of any warnings from your bank as you try to transfer the money. It should tell you if the name of the account does not match what you expect, and when this happens you should stop and check everything is as it should be. Contact your bank straight away if you have made a transfer that was not legitimate. https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/.text: Candace Savage Special to The Globe and Mail Published August 27, 2026 Open this photo in gallery: The original Treaty 6 documents are displayed at an event marking the 150th anniversary of the signing of Treaty 6, at Fort Carlton Provincial Historical Park, in Duck Lake, Sask., on Sunday. The Canadian Press Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create Free Account Candace Savage is the author of more than 25 books, including A Geography of Blood: Unearthing Memory from a Prairie Landscape , which won the Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction in 2016. A new edition of the book, with a foreward by Michelle Good, will be published in September. Every Sunday morning for the last several years, I have scrambled out of my bed here in misâskwatôhminihk (Saskatoon, Sask., in Treaty Six territory) to join other early risers from across the country in a language-learning circle known as Cree and Tea. Warmed by the kisêwâtisiwin (roughly, kindness or goodness) of the group’s co-founder, Indigenous language advocate Dr. Charlotte Ross, we sit at home in the glow of our computer screens, but with a sense that we are gathered around the same kotawân (campfire). I am of Swiss and British ancestry, with no trace of Indigenous blood, yet I always feel welcome in this company. All people come from the same fire, Charlotte reassures us; we are all wâhkôhmâkanak (relatives). If I enrolled in the group hoping to deepen my understanding of what it means, for me, to live on the Canadian Prairies, I have stayed for the generosity and beauty of Cree teachings. The main purpose of our weekly virtual get-togethers is to soak up Cree grammar and vocabulary, ē-pasikânamahk kâwih nêhiyawêwin êkwa nîhithawîwin (to lift up, or revitalize, the Plains and Woods dialects of the Cree language). In practical terms, what we mostly do is sit together and listen to Charlotte’s co-leader and nimis (older sister), Senapan Thunder, as she shares aspects of nêhiyaw mâmitonêyihciikan (Cree thought) that she has acquired through a lifelong apprenticeship to the Old Men and Old Women who were, and are, her teachers. Keeping the kotawân of Cree language and culture burning with a strong, clear flame is miyo-atoskêwin (good and purposeful). “We have come through a long time of society trying to extinguish our language,” Senapan explained at one of our sessions, her tone matter of fact. “We have come through a long time of society trying to extinguish our stories, our understandings, our prayers.” I am always amazed that she can speak of these struggles with such apparent calmness. Personally, I haven’t achieved this level of Zen. It twists my heart to know that this harm wouldn’t have happened if “society,” otherwise known as the “Crown,” or the Canadian state, had lived up to the Treaty it struck with the Indigenous peoples of central Saskatchewan and Alberta 150 years ago . Treaty Six or, as Senapan prefers to call it, wîtaskiyohtawin (Living Together on The Land) was initiated, in ceremony, at Fort Carlton, a Hudson Bay Company trading post a 100 or so kilometres north of misâskwatôhminihk on Aug. 23, 1876, and then again at Fort Pitt, near present-day Lloydminster, a couple of weeks afterwards. The lead negotiators were, on the government side, a Macdonald-era Conservative politician and true-believer in Western development, Lieutenant-Governor Alexander Morris, and on the Indigenous side, the respected Cree Chiefs Ahtahkakoop, Mistawasis and Wîhkasko-kisêyin (Sweet Grass), among others. Open this photo in gallery: Dignitaries commemorate the 150th anniversary of the signing of Treaty 6. Matt Smith/The Canadian Press For many of the Indigenous leaders in the Saskatchewan River country, this consultation was already years overdue. Although very few môniyâwak (people of European ancestry) had as yet settled in the region, their influence was being felt at a distance through smallpox epidemics and starvation. Year-by-year, the herds of plains bison, ohtâpamihowin (the means of survival), were dwindling, driven toward oblivion by a relentless slaughter. Without them, what would become of the children of this land? In presenting the provisions of the Treaty, Morris stressed the kindness of the Great Mother in this time of dire uncertainty. “The instructions of the Queen are to treat the Indians as brothers,” he told the Indigenous leaders, “and so we ought to be. The Great Spirit made this Earth we are on. He planted the trees and made the rivers flow for the good of all his people, white and red; the country is very wide and there is room for all.” Under the Treaty, Morris asserted, the Indigenous signatories would retain the freedom to maintain their hunting and fishing lifeways, while also establishing themselves as farmers. To ease this transition, the Great Mother promised to provide everything needed for success: a guaranteed land base, or reserve, plus seeds, oxen, cattle, tools and equipment. In addition, every community was promised a schoolhouse, right on the reserve, and a medicine chest, the latter an addition made at the chiefs’ request. The Indigenous leaders also negotiated a promise of relief in times of extreme hunger and distress. No problem, Morris said. “I know that the sympathy of the Queen, and her assistance, would be given you in any unforeseen circumstances,” he told the assembled chiefs. “You must trust to her generosity.” The written, English-only text of the Treaty foregrounds the extinguishment of Indigenous title to more than 300,000 square kilometres of Cree and Saulteaux territory, an area about the size of Italy or Poland. But judging from Morris’s account of the discussions, which he published in 1880 as The Treaties of Canada with the Indians of Manitoba and the North-West Territories, this subject did not come up during more than a week of discussion. The talk was all of bright days and benevolence. Most reassuring of all, this new era of equality, brotherhood and prosperity was to last forever. “As long as the sun shines and the river runs,” Morris promised. Open this photo in gallery: The Treaty 6 flag flies at Fort Carlton Provincial Historical Park. Matt Smith/The Canadian Press iskoyikohk pîsim ka-pimohtêt, iskoyikohk sîpiy ka-pimiciwahk … I was reminded of these phrases on a recent Sunday morning, when Senapan introduced a word that was new to me: sîpihkêyihtamowin . Literally rendered into English, it carries the meaning of “thinking with your heart like a river.” “That is what they used to tell us, the Old People – sîpihkêyihta ,“ Senapan said. Have the strength of mind to endure. Be very patient. “Believe in something that is higher than your physical space.” I continue to be humbled by the faith-filled, forward-flowing spirit of sîpihkêyihtamowin that has carried, and is carrying, the people of the Treaty Six First Nations through the century and a half of betrayals that have ensued since 1876. The decades of governmental neglect, ineptitude, dispossession and fraud. The multiple failures to deliver on promised benefits and to provide humanitarian aid in times of crisis. The surreal perversities of the Peasant Farming Policy and the Pass System. The cruelties of Residential Schools and the child-welfare regime. Senapan’s words echo through my thoughts: “We have come through a long time of society trying to extinguish our language, our stories, our prayers.” There are no immediate cures for this legacy of willful damage but, as I am learning through Cree and Tea, everyone and everything has the power to heal. “A heart is supposed to be happy,” Senapan says. With this encouraging instruction in mind, one task for people like me, the non-Indigenous beneficiaries of Treaty, may be to feel everything we feel about the darkness of the past (shame, grief, sorrow, fear, anger, whatever it may be) and then to set our emotional burden aside. “Heavy feelings are a veil placed over you,” Senapan teaches. “The weight you carry makes everything hazy.” In this enlightened frame of mind, perhaps we too will have the clarity to think with our hearts like a river, to advance calmly toward the future of mutual miyo-ayâwin (prosperity, health and comfort) that the Indigenous signatories of wîtaskiyohtawin envisaged for us. In doing so, we will recognize ourselves as wâhkôhmâkanak , relatives on this land, all gathered around the same kotawân . https://www.baltictimes.com/court_senten.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Court sentences Oleg Bessedin to seven years in prison 2026-09-28 BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN - The Harju County Court found Oleg Bessedin guilty under a plea agreement and sentenced him to seven years in prison. Bessedin entered into a plea agreement with the State Prosecutor's Office, under which he was convicted of two offenses: non-violent activity by a foreign national against the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the Republic of Estonia, and repeated violation of international sanctions. According to the charges, Bessedin, in coordination with Russian state structures and individuals engaged in influence operations, participated in information influence activities directed against Estonia. This involved producing and disseminating narratives justifying Russia's war of aggression, false claims, and fear-mongering rhetoric, primarily on a YouTube channel, with the aim of dividing Estonian society, eroding trust in state institutions, and undermining support for NATO and the European Union. Additionally, Bessedin repeatedly violated sanctions imposed by Council Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 by allowing the television channel TVN, which he controlled, to broadcast programs from sanctioned Russian media outlets; publishing content related to a sanctioned media outlet on his social media platform; transferring the screening rights for three of his films to a sanctioned Russian state media agency; and assisting in the launch of a television channel that broadcast content from Russian TV channels sanctioned in the EU. The court found that the agreement complied with the law, was entered into voluntarily, and approved it. The state will confiscate 77,104.32 euros of Bessedin's assets, from which procedural costs of 3,195.80 euros will also be covered as per the agreement. The ruling has not yet entered into force. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c678.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The park keeps Arctic wolves, like those pictured, and grey wolves (file image) By Lauren Turner Published 4 minutes ago An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park. She was inside an enclosure at the JohannismÃ¼hle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said. They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation". The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured. The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details. The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx. The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild. It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit. JohannismÃ¼hle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama. The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe. A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.
